title: Intelligence-Test Battery Builder
summary: Seven generic cognitive task families, one testing session, and three different purposes. Students assemble a battery under time and burden constraints, watch breadth, reliability, exposure-dependence and burden trade against each other, then see the same battery judged against all three purposes without a single task changing.
learningObjectives: Explain why validity is a property of a stated use rather than of a test.
Name the constraints that assembling a battery forces into conflict: time, breadth, reliability, exposure-dependence and burden.
Explain why composite reliability rises with test length almost regardless of what is measured, and why that makes it weak evidence of quality.
Explain why removing language from a task reduces some demands without making it independent of prior experience.
Justify a battery against a stated purpose rather than in the abstract.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native checkboxes, select and buttons throughout; each task card carries its costs as text so nothing depends on inspecting a chart. The coverage chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table that states 'not sampled' and 'barely' in words as well as by bar length. Requirements tick off in a live checklist with '(met)' / '(not yet)' written into the text. Changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: Intelligence testing: construct coverage, the trade-offs in battery construction, and validity as a property of a use
simulationNotes: Seven generic task families described in general terms; no published test, subtest, item, norm or scoring rule is reproduced, and no test is named. All values (minutes, reliability, breadth weights, exposure-dependence, burden) are illustrative and were written for this tool. Composite reliability uses Spearman-Brown on the mean task reliability and ignores intercorrelations. 'Fit to purpose' is a weighted sum invented for this tool and is not a recognised index. The tool scores batteries only: it produces no ability score for any person and simulates no group differences of any kind. Exposure-dependence is a property of a task's reliance on prior opportunity to learn its content and is never attached to a person or population.
